This document outlines the workflow of the urban phenology project. The accompanying data are available at [Zenodo](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21709425). Please download the data and place it in the `release` folder.

# Data sources

## Urban tree inventories

We first collected and cleaned the urban tree inventories from various sources, including the [McCoy's dataset](https://elifesciences.org/articles/77891), [OpenTree.org](https://opentrees.org/), and additional governmental open data portals. The codes are saved in:

-   `scripts/01_tidy_tree_inventory/tidy_elife.R`
-   `scripts/01_tidy_tree_inventory/tidy_opentree.R`

Then, species were assigned to a categorical leaf phenology type (TraitID = 37) based on the most frequently observed classification in the TRY database. The resulting summary data are stored in `release/input/tree_list/summary`.

-   `scripts/01_tidy_tree_inventory/clean_TRY_phetype.R`

Then, we futher cleaned and filtered the inventories for each city. Each city has one chunk of code, and the filtered data are stored in `release/input/tree_list`, with each city saved as one RDS file. The codes are saved in:

-   `scripts/01_tidy_tree_inventory/clean_inventories.R`
-   `scripts/01_tidy_tree_inventory/summarize_inventories.R`

The map below shows the spatial distribution of city samples. The geometry location of selected cities. The size of the circle represents the number of trees in the city.

```{r fig-inventory-map}
#| fig-cap: "spatial distribution..."
#| warning: false
inventory_centroids <- readRDS(here("release/input/tree_list/summary/inventory_centroids.rds"))
leaflet(data = inventory_centroids) |>
  addProviderTiles(providers$OpenStreetMap, options = providerTileOptions(opacity = 0.9)) |>
  addCircleMarkers(
    popup = ~ paste0(
      "<strong>", site, "</strong><br>",
      "Num individual: ", num_tree, "<br>"
    ),
    radius = ~ sqrt(num_tree/100),
    stroke = FALSE, fillOpacity = 0.5,
    color = "darkblue"
  )
```

## Climate datasets

For each tree individual, we extracted the temperature from the UHAT dataset. The codes are saved in:

-   `scripts/02_process_climate/process_UHAT.R`

We then extracted the precipitation and shortwave radiation from the Daymet dataset. The codes are saved in:

-   `scripts/02_process_climate/download_Daymet.sh`
-   `scripts/02_process_climate/process_Daymet_point.py`

The code to combine climate datasets and prepare the final tree-level climate data, stored in `release/input/tree_climate`, is:

-   `scripts/02_process_climate/prepare_tree_climate.R`

## Individual tree phenology

We followed the workflow in [Song et al. (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.srs.2025.100205) and applied package [BatchPlanet](https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.09268) to extract the phenology of individual trees:

-   Retrieved PlanetScope imagery (ortho_analytic_4b_sr) from 2017–2023 and extracted reflectance at tree coordinates.\
-   Constructed smoothed, seasonally reliable Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI) curves after computing and filtering EVI time series.
-   Extracted the timing of Start-of-season (SOS) and End-of-season (EOS) as the day of year when the growing-season EVI curves first crossed the green-up/down 50% threshold.

The processing of PlanetScope imagery is handled in the following scripts

-   `scripts/03_process_PS/download_process_PS.R` 
-   `scripts/03_process_PS/download_process_PS.sh`

The processed phenology data are stored in `release/input/phenology/doy/`. Here, we show an example of phenology extraction for an individual tree.

```{r}
#| label: fig-evi
#| fig-cap: "Example of phenology extraction for an Acer rubrum individual (40.7627°N, 73.7325°W) in New York City. Grey points show PlanetScope-derived EVI, the black line is the smoothed EVI curve. Green and orange shading indicate green-up and green-down periods, with vertical lines marking the 50% thresholds used to define SOS and EOS."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| out.width: "50%"
#| fig-align: "center"
source(here("scripts/05_plotting/plot-ps-series-example.R"))
plot_ps_series_example()
```

# Model and results

## Widespread intra-city variation in individual-tree phenology

The section is to answer the question of how large is intra-city variation in tree phenology relative to variation among cities.

### Distribution of SOS / EOS examples

The following code generates the distribution plots for SOS and EOS examples across different cities and species.

```{r}
#| eval: false
pacman::p_load(randomcoloR)
cities <- names(city_label)
set.seed(123)
color_palette <- setNames(
  distinctColorPalette(length(cities)),
  cities
)
source(here("scripts/05_plotting/plot-raw-phe.R"))

sos_species = "Pistacia chinensis" # within from large to small
sos_plots <- plot_species_raw_phe(species = sos_species, color_palette, phe_type = "SOS", color_limits = c(27, 124),
                                  highlight_city = c("LosAngeles", "NewOrleans", "Portland"), year = 2022)
example_city1_SOS <- plot_phe_one_city(city = "Portland", species = sos_species, phe_type = "SOS", year = 2022, color_limits = c(27, 124))
example_city2_SOS <- plot_phe_one_city(city = "LosAngeles", species = sos_species, phe_type = "SOS", year = 2022, color_limits = c(27, 124))
example_city3_SOS <- plot_phe_one_city(city = "NewOrleans", species = sos_species, phe_type = "SOS", year = 2022, color_limits = c(27, 124))

sos_plots$doy_map / sos_plots$sp_boxplot &
  plot_layout(heights = c(1, 0.2))

cities_SOS <- (example_city1_SOS /
  example_city2_SOS /
  example_city3_SOS)

eos_species <- "Quercus alba" # within from large to small, Tilia cordata
eos_plots <- plot_species_raw_phe(species = eos_species, color_palette, phe_type = "EOS", color_limits = c(253, 322),
                                  highlight_city = c("Atlanta", "Bloomington", "Houston"), year = 2022)

example_city1_EOS <- plot_phe_one_city(city = "Bloomington", species = eos_species, phe_type = "EOS", year = 2022, color_limits = c(253, 322))
example_city2_EOS <- plot_phe_one_city(city = "Atlanta", species = eos_species, phe_type = "EOS", year = 2022, color_limits = c(253, 322))
example_city3_EOS <- plot_phe_one_city(city = "Houston", species = eos_species, phe_type = "EOS", year = 2022, color_limits = c(253, 322))

eos_plots$doy_map / eos_plots$sp_boxplot &
  plot_layout(heights = c(1, 0.2))

cities_EOS <- (example_city1_EOS /
  example_city2_EOS /
  example_city3_EOS)
```

### Variance partitioning model

To compare the relative contributions of different sources of phenological variation, we partitioned variance in SOS and EOS into cross-city, intra-city, and cross-year components.

For species, let $y_{i,j,t}$ denote the phenological timing (SOS or EOS, day of year) of individual tree $i$ of species in city $j$ and year $t$. We fitted an intercept-only linear mixed-effects model for each species:

where:

- $\mu$ is the species-specific mean phenological timing,

- $u_{j}$ is the inter-urban (cross-city) random effect for species $m$,

- $v_{i(j)}$ is the intra-urban (cross-individual) random effect, with individuals nested within cities,

- $w_{t}$ is the interannual random effect,

- $\varepsilon_{i,j,t}$ is the residual error.

All random effects were assumed to be independent and normally distributed:

$$
y_{i,j,t}
= \mu
+ u_{j}
+ v_{i(j)}
+ w_{t}
+ \varepsilon_{i,j,t},
$$
$$
u_{j} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\mathrm{cross}}),
$$

$$
v_{i(j)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\mathrm{intra}}),
$$

$$
w_{t} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\mathrm{year}}),
$$

$$
\varepsilon_{i,j,t} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\mathrm{residual}}).
$$

The total phenological variance for species $m$ was computed as:
$$
\hat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{total}}
= \hat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{cross}}
+ \hat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{intra}}
+ \hat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{year}}
+ \hat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{residual}}.
$$

The relative contributions of spatial components were further defined as:
$$
C_{\mathrm{cross}}
= \frac{\hat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{cross}}}
{\hat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{intra}} + \hat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{cross}}},
\qquad
C_{\mathrm{intra}}
= \frac{\hat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{intra}}}
{\hat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{intra}} + \hat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{cross}}}.
$$
The model is implemented in `scripts/04_stats_model/fit_variance.R`. The resulting variance partitioning results are used to generate the figure below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-variance
#| fig-cap: "Proportional contributions of intra-city and cross-city components to variation in SOS and EOS across species."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| warning: false
source(here("scripts/05_plotting/plot-variance-ring.R"))

p_EOS_ring <- plot_variance_ring(phe_type = "EOS")
p_SOS_ring <- plot_variance_ring(phe_type = "SOS")

p_SOS_ring / p_EOS_ring +
  plot_layout(ncol = 2, 
              guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Individual-tree phenology associated with fine-scale urban temperature variation

This section investigates how is individual-tree phenology associated with fine-scale intra-city temperature variation.

### Fitting spatial models

To answer question 2, we fitted spatial statistical models separately for each species–city combination:

$$y(\mathbf{s}, t) = \mathbf{x}(\mathbf{s},t)^\top \boldsymbol{\beta}  + w(\mathbf{s}) + u(t)+ \varepsilon(\mathbf{s},t)$$

$$\mathbf{x}(\mathbf{s},t) = \left(1, \text{T}(\mathbf{s},t), \text{P}(\mathbf{s},t), \text{R}(\mathbf{s},t)\right)^\top$$

$$\boldsymbol{\beta} = (\beta_0, \beta_{\text{T}}, \beta_{\text{P}}, \beta_{\text{R}})^\top$$

$$w(\mathbf{s}) \sim \text{GP}\!\left(0,\; C(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{s}')\right)$$

$$u(t) \stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_u^2)$$

$$\varepsilon(\mathbf{s},t) \stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_\varepsilon^2)$$

$$\beta_{\ell} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\beta^2), \quad {\ell} \in \{0, {\text{T}}, {\text{P}}, {\text{R}}\}$$

The code to fit these spatial models is saved in `scripts/04_stats_model/fit_spatial/inla/run_inla_all_models.R`,
and the results are stored in `release/intermediate/spatial/inla`.

### Example spatial patterns

We show one example of the spatial patterns of mean seasonal temperature and the phenological metric for a representative species in an example city.

```{r}
#| label: fig-example
#| fig-cap: "Spatial patterns of mean seasonal temperature and the phenological metric for one representative species in one example city in 2022."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.5
source(here("scripts/05_plotting/plot-phe-temp-margin.R"))
cities = c("NewYork", "TP", "Stockton", "LosAngeles", "Seattle", "Sacramento", "WashingtonDC", "SanFrancisco")
species = c(
  "Acer rubrum", "Acer rubrum",
  "Betula pendula", "Betula pendula",
  "Liquidambar styraciflua", "Liquidambar styraciflua",
  "Acer rubrum","Acer rubrum")
phe_types = c("SOS", "SOS", "SOS", "SOS", "EOS", "EOS", "EOS", "EOS")

plot_list <- map(seq_len(1), \(i) { #8
  result <- plot_phe_temp_margin(
    city     = cities[i],
    species  = species[i],
    phe_type = phe_types[i],
    year     = 2022
  )
  result$map_panels_gridded
})
all_plots <- wrap_plots(
  plot_list
  # ncol = 2,
  # nrow = 4
) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "a")
all_plots
```

### Fitting phylogenetic generalized linear mixed models (PGLMM)

To formally assess how phenological temperature sensitivity varies with city-level climate while accounting for phylogenetic relationships among species, we fitted phylogenetic generalized linear mixed models (PGLMMs):

$$\beta_{{\text{T}},j,k}^{(r)} = \mathbf{z}_{j}^\top \boldsymbol{b} +\lambda_{k} + \varepsilon_{j,k}^{(r)} $$

$$\mathbf{z}_{j} = (1, \mathrm{MAT}_{j}, \mathrm{MAP}_{j})^\top$$

$$\boldsymbol{b} = (b_0,b_{\mathrm{MAT}},b_{\mathrm{MAP}})^\top$$

$$\boldsymbol{\lambda} = (\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_K)^\top$$

$$\boldsymbol{\lambda} \sim \mathcal{MVN}\!\left(\mathbf{0},\; \sigma^2_{\mathrm{phy}}\,\mathbf{A}\right)$$

$$\varepsilon_{j,k}^{(r)} \stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2_{\beta_\text{T}})$$

$$b_{\ell} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_b^2), \quad {\ell} \in \{0, \mathrm{MAT}, \mathrm{MAP}\}$$

```{r}
#| label: fig-coef-pglmm
#| include: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Relationships between phenological temperature sensitivity and city-level climate."
#| warning: false
source(here("scripts/04_stats_model/fit_pglmm.R"))
pglmm_path <- here("release/output/pglmm_bioclimate_inla.rds")

if (!file.exists(pglmm_path)) {
  m_SOS <- fit_multi_pglmm("SOS", input_data = df_coef, city_feature, package = "phyr", prcp = "bio12", temp = "bio1", bootstrap = T)
  m_EOS <- fit_multi_pglmm("EOS", input_data = df_coef, city_feature, package = "phyr", prcp = "bio12", temp = "bio1", bootstrap = T)
  model_list_multi <- list(m_SOS, m_EOS)
  write_rds(model_list_multi, pglmm_path)
} else {
  model_list_multi <- read_rds(pglmm_path)
}

p1 = model_list_multi[[1]][["plot"]]
p2 = model_list_multi[[2]][["plot"]] +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())

p1 + p2 +
  plot_layout(ncol = 2, guides = "collect", widths = c(1,1)) &
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```
